evidence: Campaign health plan pledges to protect Medicaid and fight federal cuts threatening ~100,000 Nevadans (2026); NV already expanded, no provider-rate plan.
Health plan would cap many drug costs at the Medicare-negotiated rate and force PBMs to pass on rebates (2026); no state board named.
Health plan pledges to drive enrollment in Battle Born State Plans, Nevada's new public option, with an outreach campaign (2026).
Health plan would relieve medical debt for those under 400% FPL via nonprofits and ban reporting medical debt to credit agencies (2026).
Health plan backs a bipartisan prior-authorization reform, including barring AI-only denials (2026); reform, not elimination.
Would pause data center tax breaks until commitments are met and require them to supply their own power, grid upgrades and water (2026).
Energy plan would stop NV Energy's residential daily demand charge and put consumer advocates on the PUC (2026); no fee cap or lobbying-cost ban.
Housing plan would cut permitting red tape, set statewide housing goals and standards, and open ~10,000 vacant acres to building (2026).
Housing plan would boost down payment aid for first-time buyers via refundable tax credits (2026); no broker-fee ban.
Housing plan would cap security deposits at one month's rent, ban junk fees and bar algorithmic rent-fixing (2026).
Housing plan would cap annual corporate-investor home purchases and create a corporate landlord registry (2026).
Campaign said in Aug 2026 he will not raise taxes during the affordability crisis; no comment on a millionaire tax specifically.
Opposes public money for private schools and wants K-12 per-pupil funding raised to the national average (May 2026).
Sponsored a 2017 paid sick leave expansion (vetoed); campaign signaled support for expanding it (Jun 2026). Sick leave, not a PFML program.
As Senate majority leader he advanced a 2017 minimum wage hike bill that was vetoed (cited Jun 2026); no $15 pledge found.
Pledges to root out fraud, waste and abuse and let Medicaid open fraud probes on its own (2026); no inspector general proposal.
Supports enshrining abortion rights through 24 weeks in the Nevada Constitution (Aug 2026).
Day-one Executive Order 1 declared a utility-cost emergency and froze electric rate hikes (Jan 2026); later added $25 and $150 bill credits (Jul 2026).
Her administration is pressing PJM for a price collar to stabilize power costs over four years (Jul 2026). Prior evidence (BPU pause) was a rate-freeze item, not a price cap.
Signed the Data Center Fair Share Act (S731), creating a separate rate class so data centers pay for their own power and grid costs (Jul 2026).
Signed bills repealing the utility ROE adder and requiring state approval of supplemental transmission projects (Jul 2026); no fee cap or lobbying-cost ban.
FY2027 budget adds $5 million to down payment assistance for about 3,000 first-time buyers (Mar 2026); no broker-fee ban.
FY2027 budget raises revenue partly by paring back corporate tax loopholes while funding $4.2B in property-tax relief (Mar 2026); the two are not formally tied.
FY2027 budget funds $4.2B in property-tax relief (ANCHOR, Senior Freeze, Stay NJ) and caps Stay NJ eligibility at $250K income (Mar 2026).
FY2027 budget maintains the state Child Tax Credit, EITC and dependent care credit (Mar 2026); no expansion proposed.
FY2027 budget puts $582M into child care assistance to fully reopen CCAP applications (Mar 2026); not a universal system.
FY2027 budget proposes a record $1.4B in Preschool Education Aid (Mar 2026); no universal pre-K pledge found.
FY2027 budget proposes a record $12.4B for K-12 schools, up $370M, and a school-funding formula overhaul (Mar 2026); no voucher statement found.
FY2027 budget was built on a rule of no new taxes on everyday New Jerseyans (Mar 2026); no millionaire-tax proposal.
FY2027 budget keeps $7.2B for NJ FamilyCare covering 1.8M residents and aids counties hit by federal H.R. 1 changes (Mar 2026); NJ already expanded.
Feb 2026 Executive Order 12 bars ICE from nonpublic state property, incl. residential medical sites and child care centers, without a judicial warrant; narrower than the measure.
Signed HB 245 lifting the 2025 sunset and continuing Montana's Medicaid expansion (Mar 2025); no provider-rate increase noted.
Signed 2023 pro-housing zoning laws forcing big cities to allow duplexes and backyard units, dubbed the "Montana Miracle" (cited Oct 2024).
Vetoed a 2021 state housing tax credit bill and says the state cannot buy its way out of the shortage (cited Oct 2024); a related, not identical, tool.
Signed SB 542 and HB 231 creating a lower Homestead Rate for primary residences and long-term rentals plus up to $400 rebates (2025; touted Nov 2025).
Signed HB 337 cutting income tax rates and widening the lower 4.7% bracket (Apr 2025); a broad flat-tax move, not middle-class targeted.
Signed HB 337, which doubles Montana's earned income tax credit (Apr 2025), after expanding it in 2023.
Signed and touts the 2021 TEACH Act, which pays districts incentives to raise starting teacher salaries (cited Oct 2024).
Opposed CI-128, the 2024 ballot measure writing abortion rights into the Montana Constitution (2024); it passed.
In his 2026 State of the State he hailed pro-life laws and the anti-abortion constitutional amendment as protecting more babies than any time since Roe (Jan 2026).
Touted that Nebraska under his watch stopped taxing seniors' Social Security income (State of the State, Jan 2026).
Cited expanded property-tax relief and a cap on local tax collections and called for more (Jan 2026); relief is broad, not specifically targeted.
Faulted past tax policy for carveouts and loopholes, but wants tax cuts paid for by spending cuts and proposed a new 10% business tax credit (Jan 2026).
Was first governor to opt into the federal Scholarship Tax Credit for private and homeschool students, calling it a gamechanger (Jan 2026).
Celebrated Nebraska's ICE detention facility and partnership with Trump on enforcement (Jan 2026); no stance on sensitive-location limits.
Pushes running government like a business to cut fraud, waste and abuse, citing $141M HHS savings and $30M Medicaid recoveries (Jan 2026); no inspector general plan.
Signed 2025 laws setting a 60-day local permitting clock, expanding ADUs and allowing business-to-housing conversions; called housing her top priority (2026 State of the State).
Campaign pledged to keep NH's current law allowing abortion up to 24 weeks and to veto new restrictions (2024); no support for codifying a right found.
2026 State of the State highlighted keeping NH Medicaid eligibility at New England-leading levels and funding the disability waitlist; NH already expanded.
2026 State of the State faulted the PUC for accommodating utilities and urged regulators to hold utilities accountable to ratepayers; no fee cap or lobbying limit.
2026 State of the State called for more affordable child care and proposed a tax credit for employers investing in staff child care; not a universal system.
Expanded Education Freedom Accounts to universal eligibility (touted in 2026 State of the State) after campaigning for universal education freedom (2024).
2024 campaign site pledged to improve pay and benefits for high-performing educators; no across-the-board raise plan.
2024 campaign site vowed she will never allow an income or sales tax in New Hampshire, which would bar a millionaire income tax.
Campaigned on zero tolerance for sanctuary cities (2024) and cited banning them in her 2026 State of the State; no sensitive-location stance.
Created a Commission on Governmental Efficiency and proposed fee refunds when agencies miss deadlines (2026 State of the State); no inspector general plan.
